description: Our team aims to develop innovative, practical solutions to real-world challenges through technology. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we’re focusing on an astronaut health monitoring system combining real-time data processing, intelligent alerts, and an intuitive dashboard to support astronaut health and safety during space missions.
summary:
MissionVitals is a self-check health app for astronauts on long missions, built for a crew tablet. On a trip to Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, so the crew can’t wait for a flight surgeon to tell them whether a reading is a problem. MissionVitals lets each astronaut see their own health, understand it and act on it.

It tracks nine indicators linked to NASA’s human spaceflight hazards: heart rate, SpO₂, blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose, sleep, exercise, mood and habitat radiation. A body figure shows where each reading belongs. Every reading has one of five statuses, In range, Watch, Caution, Warning or No data, always shown with an icon and a word as well as a colour. When something is out of range, the app gives plain steps: re-measure, rest, check the sensor, then escalate to the crew medical officer or to Earth. Reports wait in a queue when the Earth link is down.

Guided procedures cover each manual measurement. A daily routine, a symptom log and a crew overview with privacy rules complete it. The solar storm scenario replays real flare, CME and particle-event timing from NASA’s DONKI records of May 2024. A Node API stores entries in Postgres and falls back to local mode if the server is lost. Readings are simulated and thresholds are demo values, not medical advice.
details:
MissionVitals is a tablet-first web app that lets an astronaut check their own health, understand what the numbers mean, and know what to do next, without waiting for Earth. On a Mars mission a one-way message can take up to 22 minutes, so the first response to a bad reading has to happen on board.

What it does
The astronaut picks their name on a shared crew tablet; there is no login. My Health shows nine indicators grouped by NASA’s human spaceflight hazards. Heart rate, SpO₂ and exercise come live from a sensor shirt. Blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose, sleep and mood are entered by the astronaut. Habitat radiation comes from a dosimeter. A clickable body figure shows where each reading belongs. Each indicator has one of five statuses: In range, Watch, Caution, Warning or No data. A status is always shown with an icon and a word, never by colour alone. Selecting a reading opens what to do now, a trend chart, and why it changes in space. Advice escalates in three steps: yourself, the crew medical officer, then the flight surgeon on Earth. Guided procedures walk through each manual measurement, and a daily routine shows what is due. There is also a symptom log on the body figure and a crew overview. Symptoms and mood are private to the astronaut and the crew medical officer. Reports to Earth show the real link delay and wait in a queue while the link is down.

How it works
The app is React and TypeScript, built with Vite. A Node API runs as a Vercel function and stores everything the astronaut enters in Postgres (Supabase). That covers readings, symptoms, routine actions, alert acknowledgements and reports. On a spacecraft the same database would run on the onboard server. Status rules live in one shared package used by both the browser and the server, so they always agree. Live readings come from a seeded simulator. If the server can’t be reached, the app switches to local mode and says so. Losing the onboard server and losing the Earth link are shown as separate states. Every demo session is isolated, so judges never see each other’s data.

Real NASA data
The solar storm scenario replays the flare, coronal mass ejection and GOES particle arrivals of the May 2024 storm. The timing and links come from NASA’s DONKI records, and habitat radiation rises with them. The dose rate itself is simulated, because DONKI records events, not dose. The app labels clearly what is real and what is simulated.

Design choices

  • Alert levels, acknowledgement, and silencing an alarm by acting on it follow NASA’s crew alert design guidance.
  • The status colours were checked for colour blindness and for contrast in light and dark mode.
  • The app was tested with axe-core accessibility checks.
  • It works on a tablet, a laptop and a phone, with keyboard support and reduced motion.
  • Every threshold is labelled a demo value. The app gives steps, not diagnoses.
  • Seven demo scenarios and four mission settings (Mars transit, space station, lunar base, Mars rover) show how it behaves.

Impact
MissionVitals turns raw readings into clear actions and keeps the crew informed when Earth is minutes away. The same approach suits remote clinics, Antarctic stations and ships.

Tools
TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Radix UI, Lucide icons, React Router, Zod, Node.js, Supabase (Postgres), Vercel, Vitest, Playwright and axe-core. Code was written with Claude Code (AI-assisted) and reviewed and edited by me. Solo entry by Zac Lehmann.
